questions.prompt: What is the difference between try, try?, and try! in Swift? When should each be used? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains try is used inside do-catch or throwing functions to propagate or catch errors
Explains try? converts thrown errors into nil, returning an Optional
Explains try! asserts success and crashes at runtime if an error is thrown

questions.modelAnswer: In Swift, try is used inside do-catch blocks or throwing functions to propagate errors to the caller. The try? keyword converts the result into an optional, evaluating to nil if an error is thrown without requiring a do-catch block. The try! keyword asserts that no error will occur, unwrapping the result immediately but crashing if an error is thrown.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Error Handling

questions.prompt: Why are Swift enumerations with associated values well suited for modeling errors? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that enums model a discrete set of related error conditions
States that associated values attach relevant diagnostic context to specific cases
Mentions that callers can use pattern matching in catch clauses to inspect details

questions.modelAnswer: Swift enumerations are ideal for error modeling because they define a clear, closed set of related error cases. Enums can include associated values to attach specific diagnostic details, such as an HTTP status code or missing file path. Callers can then use pattern matching in catch blocks to handle specific failure modes with full type safety.

questions.prompt: Explain how the defer keyword works in Swift. In what order do multiple defer blocks in the same scope execute? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that defer delays execution of a block until the surrounding scope is exited
States that defer runs regardless of whether the scope exits normally or by throwing an error
Explains that multiple defer statements execute in reverse order (last in, first out)

questions.modelAnswer: The defer keyword schedules code to run just before the current scope exits. It is guaranteed to run whether the function returns normally, breaks early, or throws an error. When multiple defer blocks exist in the same scope, they execute in reverse order, running the last declared defer statement first.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Error Handling

questions.prompt: How does Swift error handling differ from exception handling in languages like Java or C++? Answer in 2–4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift error handling does not unwind the call stack
States that errors are passed as typed values using registers with the speed of a return statement
Notes that try marks throwing call sites explicitly for compile-time safety

questions.modelAnswer: Unlike Java or C++, Swift error handling does not unwind the call stack. Instead, Swift passes errors as lightweight typed values, matching the runtime performance of a standard return statement. The Swift compiler requires explicit try annotations at every throwing call site, ensuring that error paths are visible and checked at compile time.

rubric.criterion: Defines Result as an enumeration with success and failure cases
Explains that Result captures the outcome of an operation as a first-class value

questions.modelAnswer: The Result type is a standard library enumeration with success and failure cases. It stores the outcome of an operation as a first-class value in memory. Result is often preferred over throwing functions when passing results across asynchronous completion handlers or storing outcomes for later evaluation.
